cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: Christ, haloed and with outstretched arms, rises from a green hill and draws up a crowd of people who cluster around him, while the sun and moon appear in the sky. The verse above reads 'Save thy people, and bless thine inheritance: feed them also, and lift them up for ever'.
facts: The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

cur:objects2-tsilkani-icon.summary: The Virgin, in a dark red maphorion, holds the Christ Child on her left arm and gestures toward him, while two archangels with staffs stand at her shoulders. The large-eyed, solemn faces are framed by a metal revetment set with medallions. From the monastery of Tsilkani in eastern Georgia, it is one of the oldest icons of the Georgian Church.
facts: Tsilkani is an early Christian monastery in the historic region of Kartli in eastern Georgia.
Commons gives the date as 9th century; the icon is now kept in the Art Museum of Georgia in Tbilisi.
cur:objects2-tsilkani-icon.notes: The dating of the painted panel and of its revetment is debated; some scholars place the painting earlier. Medium given in general terms.

walters:71.305.summary: Set against the silhouette of a mountain, the Virgin reclines on a great mattress beside the manger where the swaddled Christ Child lies, watched by the ox and the ass beneath a ray of light from above. Angels emerge from behind the mountain, one announcing the birth to a shepherd leaning on his staff at the right, while in the foreground Joseph sits pensively as two women give the haloed infant his first bath. The carving gathers the whole Christmas story into one luminous scene.
facts: The Walters notes that the bathing of the newborn Christ is characteristic of Byzantine images of the Nativity and rarely appears in western European art.
The plaque was owned by Count Girolamo Possenti of Fabriano before 1876 and later by Count Grigorii Stroganov in Rome.
